original_question: For every epsilon > 0, does there exist a constant kappa(epsilon) such that whenever a, b, c are pairwise coprime positive integers with a + b = c, one has c < kappa(epsilon) R(abc)^(1 + epsilon)?
correct_elements: Your draft is very close to the paper's official formulation: it has the right quantifier structure ('for every epsilon > 0'), the correct dependence on a constant kappa(epsilon), the correct Diophantine relation a + b = c, the intended positivity/integrality of a, b, c, and the correct bound c < kappa(epsilon) R(abc)^(1+epsilon). Its 'pairwise coprime' wording is also compatible with the paper's coprimality hypothesis in this setting.
missing_details: The notation R(n) must be defined explicitly: in Section 2.1 the paper sets R(n) = ∏_{p|n} p, the radical (square-free part) of the positive integer n.
To match the paper exactly, the ambient domain should be stated as positive integers ('positive rational integers' in the paper's wording), i.e. ordinary integers in Z_{>0}.
The paper's exact coprimality phrase is that a, b, c are 'relatively prime'; for a stand-alone formulation, writing gcd(a,b,c)=1 is the most faithful explicit version.
The paper states that kappa(epsilon) is a positive number depending only on epsilon.
No extra ordering such as 0 < a < b < c is part of Conjecture 2.1; such orderings appear only later when the paper lists notable examples.
refined_question: Let R(n) = ∏_{p|n} p denote the radical (square-free part) of a positive integer n. Is it true that for every epsilon > 0 there exists a positive constant kappa(epsilon) such that for all positive integers a, b, c with gcd(a,b,c) = 1 and a + b = c, one has c < kappa(epsilon) R(abc)^(1+epsilon)?
justification: The draft is targeting exactly the abc conjecture as stated at the start of Section 2.1: the paper first defines the radical R(n), then gives Conjecture 2.1 in essentially the same form as your draft. The nearby context introduces the auxiliary quantities lambda(a,b,c) and rho(a,b,c) only to discuss examples, and then moves on to consequences such as Szpiro's conjecture and the Erdos-Woods problem, not to an equivalent reformulation. So the sharpest paper-faithful rewrite is simply Conjecture 2.1 itself, made fully self-contained by defining R and spelling out the coprimality condition.
